name: Weber's Law / Just Noticeable Difference
description: A change becomes noticeable only once it exceeds a threshold relative to the current stimulus level — the classic just-noticeable-difference idea. Designers often use it to reason about how much visual, motion, haptic, or pricing change users will actually perceive.
design_relevance_note: Used when tuning motion, spacing, color, haptics, loading feedback, personalization, and price or plan changes that teams want users to notice — or not notice — at particular magnitudes.
myth_risk_note: The classical Weber-Fechner law as commonly stated does not hold precisely; intensity discrimination shows more complex patterns than a simple logarithmic relationship.
prevalence_note: A standard reference point in interaction-design, perception, and HCI-adjacent teaching, though not as universally cited in everyday UX discourse as Fitts's or Hick's Law.

findings.description: Reviewing decades of psychophysics research, including the authors' own neural studies of texture/roughness perception, this review found that Weber's law (constant-ratio just-noticeable-differences) is often not valid — not a weakness of Fechner's broader framework, the review argues, but evidence that the actual underlying relationship between neural activity and subjective experience is linear, not logarithmic, once measured directly at the neural level rather than inferred indirectly from behavior alone.
findings.source_title: Review: Neural Coding and the Basic Law of Psychophysics

findings.description: The classic Weber-Fechner law holds that a stimulus change only becomes perceptible once it exceeds a fixed proportion of the stimulus's current magnitude (a 'just noticeable difference'), and Fechner used this to derive a logarithmic relationship between physical stimulus intensity and subjective perceived intensity — the basis for design/pricing folklore about gradual, below-threshold changes going unnoticed.
findings.source_title: Review: Neural Coding and the Basic Law of Psychophysics
